Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
So with a good turnout of 11 total players (Howard swapped in for
Sackett in the draft round), Keith Rice came out of VTES retirement to
bring Evil Vampire Barbie back to Binghamton for the second time in 5
years, securing victory with a devestating "win the tie breaker die
roll" gambit that no one saw coming!.

In 3 rounds of play (2 rounds of constructed, 1 round of 4 booster
pack Jyhad draft), the 11 players and their total VPs were:

-Keith Rice: 10 VP
-Josh Duffin: 10 VP
-Jon Darbro: 4 VP
-Dave (who's last name I can never remeber): 2 VP
-Luke Gabriel: 1 VP
-Howard Sanders: 1 VP
-Eric Howd; 0
-Jay Davis: 0
-Jason Dettman: 0
-Andrew Sackett; 0
-Peter Bakija: 0

Keith kicked ass with total old school decks, including a Nosferatu
Prince Rush deck and a Brujah Prince breed/vote deck. I don't think he
had even any Sabbat cards in his decks, and was heard saying in some
game "What kinda vampire is Sacha Viklos? I don't think I have ever
even seen that clan..."

Josh kicked ass with new school decks, including an Arika Zillah's
Valley/Parity Shift deck and a Pistolero Cel/Disguised Magnum deck.

At the end of the three rounds, Josh and Keith were tied with 10 VPs
each (and according to Josh, they had the same theoretical tournament
point score) and rather than coming up with a better way to determine
the winner, they rolled a die, and Keith rolled a 6 vs Josh's 2.

The theme for the evening, however, seemed to be "Josh drove 6 hours
to come and hose me!" In the first round, Josh was my predator, and he
beat me down pretty well with Parity Shifts, PTO'ed my Cicatriz, and
then Kindred Restructured the table so that he was my prey allowing
Jon's Cryptic Mission deck ("I must bring this cheese to Washington!
Immediately!) to oust me and eventually win the table with a 3 VP
withdraw (Jon is, after all, the master of withdrawing!). Game 2, due
to the wonders of my fabulous random seating procedure (I rolled
dice...), Josh is my prey, and manages to convince his prey, Jason, to
rush cross table and mess me up a bunch (through the judicious use of
the "I give him 2 pool through his Succubus Club" manuver, which
somehow convinced Jason that Rushing cross table to hose me was a good
idea), which tools my already tenious position. Later that game, Jason
attempts to fix his earlier error by giving me all of his pool and
permanents with the Succubs Club after Josh was about to oust him, but
it didn't really help. In the third round of draft, 'cause the Fates
weren't done being amused, Josh sat across table from me, and with his
very first action in the game was to Disputed Territory my Backways
away from me. And it just went down hill from there.

The big observations from the evening:

-Why is Succubus Club still allowed in competetive play? The card is
just stoopid.

-Why does Protect Thine Own still exist in its current form? The card
is just stoopid.

-Why is Josh still allowed in competetive play? He's broken.

Thanks to everyone who showed up, and now Keith needs to make sure and
come back next year so he can defend Evil Vampire Barbie. Luckily, he
apprently won't need to practice in the interm.

-Peter

Heh. If I could have killed Josh, I would have in a second :-)

The situation was this (which I am mostly describing to illustrate my
issues with the Succubus Club):

The table was Me (CEL/+1 strength deck); Josh (weenie cel/pistols
Rush); Jason (Assamite long range Rush); Jay (Toreador bleed).

Jason plays Succubus Club. On Josh's next turn, he says "Jason, I'll
give you 2 pool if you mess up Peter's Aziz." Jason is Josh's prey. I
am Jason's cross table "ally". Jay is in the middle, not really going
anywhere, but not really getting ousted soon. Jason agrees. On Jason's
turn, he takes the 2 pool from Josh, Rushes and torporizes Aziz. In
terms of overall table dynamic, this did nothing to help Jason (except
get him the 2 pool from his predator), did everything to help Josh
(Josh's prey wasted an action to kill his predator's vampire), and
totally tooled me (and I was in a tenious position to begin with). Was
this cheating? Collusion? 'Cause I was playing with people I know, it
I know it wasn't collusion, it was just Jason being Jason. But if I
were playing with strangers, I'd have been far more irritated by this
action that was basically permited by the Succubus Club.

Right. I get tooled. The game moves on, Josh is clearly winning. I
convince Jason to rush back at Josh (by offering him 2 pool...). Jason
does so, and gets most of his vampires torpored. Jason becomes
hoplessly crippled. In an act of remorse, he uses Succubus Club to
give me all of his vampires, stuff, and all but 1 of his (5 or 6
remaining) pool. Sadly, it doesn't help me much, as I am already in a
horrible position and not going anywhere, but the stuff Jason gives me
keeps me in the fight a couple extra turns. At this point, realizing I
was hosed, I should have used Succubus Club (which I had inherreted
from Jason) to give Jay (who was still alive, but mostly a non issue
at this point) all my pool, vampires, and stuff, to put Jay back in
the game.

All this silliness was allowed by the Succubus Club. Yeah, one could
claim that the problem was that Jason is broken, and not the Succubus
Club, but we can't fix him :-)

Succubus Club is not broken 'cause it is too "powerful". It is simply
inappropriate for competetive play, as it allows for too many outside
factors to come into play, and requires too much arbitration--every
time I have seen the Succubus Club used, it has been used in a way
that could be argued to be collusive (i.e. cheating). I don't think I
have ever seen the Succubus Club used for any mundane purpose (i.e.
"Hey--I'll trade you a Blood Doll for a Potence Master..."). It is
always something very game affecting, and always something
questionable, bordering on collusive.

Jason taking pool from his predator to demolish his predator's
predator in an action that is clearly detrimental to his position is
something that, if it happened in a serious competetive environment,
would end up having a Judge called over. Jason then driving the last
nail into his coffin by giving away all his stuff and all but 1 of his
pool would result in the same. Me deciding to oust myself to then give
all my pool to my predator as I wasn't going anywhere anyway, and I
was filled with spite, would similarly result in arbitration I'm sure.

How is it good to have a card in serious competition that results in
such a need for arbitration? Again, I have seen *far* more disputes
and post game accusations of collusion result from the use of Succubus
Club than anything else in this game.

Yeah, we could simply call for a judge in every possible instance
where we feel that Succubus Club is being used inappropriately, but
that then requires far more judgement than simple rules disputes--"Can
this card be used for X?" is a much easier issue to deal with than "My
opponent's are cheating! I want them ejected! They did X with the
Succubus Club...", and requires arbitrary decisions to be made that
there is only the most vague guidance for.

Again, any game suffers from the need for too much arbitration.
Succubus Club potentially requres more arbitration than any other card
in the game. It strikes me that it would be far more beneficial to
remove it as a source of conflict than leave it in.

-Peter

you are "dead", you can do anything you want, but you are then randomly
acting against your own best interest (i.e. staying alive and trying to oust
your prey) in the name of someone else, which someone could always argue to
be collusion. Say I sit down at a game with a friend of mine who is across
the table. I'm losing and close to ousted, so I use my Succubus Club to give
my friend all my stuff. I could argue that I'm doing it to help the table
against the guy in the lead. Everyone else at the table could argue that I'm
doing it 'cause he is my friend, and I'm acting on out of game consideration
("If I can't win, at least my freind can..."), which falls under the VEKN
rules on collusion, which is a form of cheating.

Yeah, this sort of thing can happen without the Succubus Club, sure, but
generally to a much less tangible/significant/concrete effect.

> As long as they are

> the play.

I'm sure someone could argue about the legality of anything. And most
actions facilitated by SC are something that someone could (and probably
should) argue. Yeah, if I'm dying, and I give all my stuff to someone across
the table, that may or may not be collusion. What if I give all my stuff to
my predator? That is clearly against the spirit of the rules (getting myself
killed to bolster my main opponent?), yet may or may not be collusion. What
if he is a play group mate of mine?

> I'd say that many games reach a point where 2 or more players realize that one
> particular person is waaay ahead and will almost certainly win. They may even
> wish to gang up on the leader. The pred/prey relationship keeps the amount of
> ganging-up that is possible to a limit.

The game was specifically designed to minimize king-makerness, which is one
of the reasons that VTES is such a good game...

> The SC, IMO, just takes the desire to
> gang-up and instantly enables the kinds of sharing of resources that makes
> squashing the leader much easier.

...yet the Succubus Club is thrown into the mix and its only purpose is to
completely circumvent all the anti-king-maker safeguards in the game. VTES
is a good multi player game 'because it was designed specifically to
minimize the main hazzards of multi player games. Succubus Club just goes
and aggrivates them again. How is this good?

> I think that's going a bit far in my experience. I really don't like the card
> but I think this is a little strong.

Certainly my statement was hyperbolic, but not that far off. The VEKN
tournament rules include pretty detailed rules to prevent cheating and
unsportsmanlike conduct (5.1 and 5.2), including "collusion to alter the
results of a game". Acting against your own best interests to aid someone
else across the table (or next to you) by giving them all your stuff through
the Succubus Club is certainly something that could be argued to be
"collusion to alter the results of a game"--why is it ok that if, say, I am
winning the game by virtue of good play and a good deck, that someone use
the Succubus Club to ruin their own game help someone else defeat me? What
if those two people are friends (i.e. have a pre-existing relationship)?
What if the guy giving away all the stuff was someone that I had ousted and
beat in a previous game? Would I not be justified in calling a judge to
arbitrate the deal? Is this something we want to saddle judges with in the
first place?

> BTW, I did play the club in my qualifying deck and my Weenie Potence deck that
> got to the GenCon finals a couple years ago. It was included basically to
> contest other SC's--which I did twice. I also rampaged one of them. I also
> got bit in the arse once when David Tatu played one and his predator passed
> all his remaining pool and minions to David just before I was going to oust
> him.

Which is what the SC facilitates. It pretty much does nothing *but*
facilitate this sort of tom-foolery.

If the Succubus Club allowed for very limited trades (say, you could trade 1
vampire for 1 vampire or 1 card in hand for 1 card in hand or 1 non vampire
card in play for 1 non vampire card in play), it would still be useful and
fun, but it wouldn't allow for the "Hmm. I'm losing. I'm going to randomly
give all my pool, vampires, and master cards in play to my predator in
exchange for nothing, just 'cause I don't like the guy who is currently in
the lead..." that is more often than not the end result of a Succubus Club
use.

The card is simply inappropriate for serious competetive play. It allows for
too concrete an effect to king-making and facilitates/encourages collusion,
which the VEKN rules (and the basic VTES rules) go out of their way to
limit. The use of the card should be completely over taxing and irritating
the hell out of judges, which is something they don't need. It is just a bad
card for competetive play.

Say I'm your grand prey. You say "Give me 2 pool, and I'll attack your
predator (i.e. your prey)..." I'm not giving you pool--you are going
to attack them anyway. If you say "Hey, predator--give me pool and I
won't attack your minions...", your predator will ignore you, as you
are going to attack his minions anyway as soon as he starts to hurt
you, which is his job in the forst place.

If your grand prey *doesn't* give you pool to attack your prey, what
are you going to do? Attack *his* vampires? All that does is waste
your actions and make it easier for your prey to oust him (i.e. it is
counter productive)

In the end, I'd think that most people that you threaten will (or
should) simply ignore you.

> I think the key lesson to be learned about the Succubbus Club
> is that you use it, don't let it determine what you do. Ideally you
> can use the Succubbus Club to get paid for rushes you were going to do
> anyways.

How? Jedi mind tricks? If someone says "Hey--give me pool and I'll
attack my prey's vampires", I'm not giving them pool. If they threaten
to attack me cross table unless I give them pool, I also ignore them
(or at least appeal to their sense of logic)--attacking across table
to punish people for not paying is not a strategy that leads to
winning. It is a strategy that leads to someone else winning.

> It doesn't always work out that way, but I think you'd be
> surprised how much *free* pool the SC can generate.

I'd be surprised if it generated any pool at all. I can't for the life
of me figure out why people would pay up in the situations you
describe.

Rush decks are difficult to win with. They are even more difficult to
win with if you waste effort rushing cross table, especially as you
are simply making it easier for someone else to win at the same time.
Yeah, you could threaten to do this unless people pay you, but if they
don't pay, what do you do? If you live up to your threat, you are
probably hurting yourself in the long run (wasting actions, incurring
wrath, strengthening the position of other players in a way that
doesn't benefit you). Are you then going to kill *all* of their
vampires? Now that you threatened some guy across the table, he didn't
pay up, and you killed his vampire, you don't think for a second that
he is now, out of spite, going to Deflect every bleed he can at you or
target you with every damaging vote? This is the key to a winning
strategy? Make *everyone* mad at you?

Again, Rush decks can do this without Succubus Club. And it usually
makes them lose. Adding Succubus Club does little more than encourage
reckless play, and still doesn't make you win.

-Peter

you will do whatever it is that your deck does to oust your prey
(discounting moving the table around, which you really can't discount),
but that doesn't mean that you will necessarily do it *right now*. I'm
not saying that your way of playing, the "rabid auto-crush", can't be
successful, but it is *not* the One True Way.

Same deal with the predator. Personally, I *don't* erase my predator
backwards at the first sign of a hard bleed. If he's amassed enough
resources to go for the one turn kill then, sure, he's due for some
trimming. But accepting the fact that your predator is going to do
predator things, and that you are going to lose some pool because of it,
and being able to not tilt the table out of whack just because you can, is
an important step in developing successful rush strategies.

Perhaps you have a bit of a self-fulfilling prophecy going on?

> In the end, I'd think that most people that you threaten will (or
> should) simply ignore you.

Did you know that the early work in game theory was flawed by the
assumption of perfectly rational participants? That it was also flawed by
an assumption of perfect knowledge of an opponent's moves and resources?

> attack my prey's vampires", I'm not giving them pool. If they threaten
> to attack me cross table unless I give them pool, I also ignore them
> (or at least appeal to their sense of logic)--attacking across table
> to punish people for not paying is not a strategy that leads to
> winning. It is a strategy that leads to someone else winning.

So you don't think the "carrot and the stick" exist? Have you never
extracted a little something from that spare point of KRC damage? You get
those things because you are in a position of strength and the stick
exists. Other players pretending the stick *doesn't* exist are, arguably,
playing in an irrational manner that you claim to dislike. Say I've got
rushes out the wazoo, one way or another. Say my prey is *not* playing a
weenie deck. In fact, there are no weenie decks on the table, so I've got
rushes to spare. If I can expend something I have in abundance, and in
return take something away from someone who can't afford to lose it, how
is it not "rational" for them to deal? Maybe they don't like it, maybe
they think I'm a thug, but other players getting pissy and throwing the
game on those grounds is not *my* fault.

Nobody throws a hissy about KRC damage, or Parity Shift pool, spreading
around outside the pred-prey triangle. What you've got isn't a rational
argument, it's an irrational reaction to rush. Once we've shown that
irrationality is at the heart of the whole issue, I think you need to go
back and re-examine your strategy in light of the possibility that people
are going to behave that way.

That, and the timing issue, which is probably more key and more objective,
but I gotta go.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Ira wrote:
> A rules question: if I have a leather jacket in play and I use
> Succubus Club to give it to another Methuselah, how do they make use
> of it? They don't get to put it on one of their minions, do they?
> Perhaps they can take an action to move it to one of their minions?

When control of an equipment card, a retainer, or an on-minion location
changes, in an ambiguous fashion (that is, the effect that changes
control doesn't also explicitly say where to move the card, as in the
case of a Succubus Club trade), the new controller puts the card on one
of her ready minions.

When control of any other card is changed, the card doesn't move (unless
the effect changing control says to move it).

description to individual turns, then negotiating a particular turn to

not inherently irrational to deal in such a way that you appear to be

> I thought you were trying to find a solution that would stop what

Correct. The only reasonable way to do this, as far as I can see (as
by reasonable, I mean non ambigiously and with limited wordage) is by
rewording the card to include hard, strict limits on what could be
traded, including a maximum pool limit (as one of the largest abuses
of SC seems to stem from arbitrarily ousting one's self by giving away
all your pool when you are in a losing position). With hard,
unambigious limits, there is no SC hanky-panky that results in needing
arbitration and taxing the judges. Or at least much less.

>Paying 10 for Arika is a
> legit trade.

As Josh pointed out, not necessarily. Giving someone Arika with a
flame thrower could be a *huge* swing in power that could be seen as
nothing more than collusion. And if 10 pool is legitimate for such a
trade, and the SC allows for such a trade, how do you keep someone
from trading 10 pool for, say, a Short Term Investement when it only
has 1 counter and they only have 10 pool?

Yes, limiting trades to a maximum of, say, 2 pool (or 1 or 3 or
whatever) would prevent trading Arika with a Flamethrower for 10 pool
(which could be argued to be a legitimate trade). But that strikes me
as perfectly reasonable--large legitimate trades are removed as a
possibility, which is sad, but large, preposterous trades that
completely throw the balance of the game and are arguably the result
of collusion are removed as a possibility too. Which is only good.

If strict limits are put on the card, there is always going to be a
trade that seems legitimate, yet is outside the realm of what the card
permits. If the upper limit of pool being traded is, say, 2, then
yeah, you can't make the arguably legitimate trade of Arika and a
Flamethrower for 10 pool. But if the upper limit of pool being traded
away is set at 10, then you couldn't make the arguably legitimate
trade of Arika, a Flame Thrower, The Rack, a Flak Jacket, The Eye of
Hazimel, a Sport Bike, The Soul Gem, and a Assault Rifle for 15 pool,
which also seems like a legitimate trade. Which is sad, but an
unambigious line needs to be set somewhere if the card is to be
reigned in.

-Peter
